youtube.title: Do the Moon's footprints last? | One More Orbit · Season 2 · Episode 6
youtube.caption:
Do the Moon's footprints last? Look closer.

The Moon has almost no air or rain, so prints wear away very slowly; an orbiter has photographed the Apollo 11 site. Some prints may still be there.

Series: One More Orbit · Season 2 · Episode 6.

Sources
1. Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969; the astronauts walked on the surface. — nasa.gov: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/apollo-11/
2. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has imaged the Apollo 11 landing site: the descent stage and the astronauts' trails are visible. — science.nasa.gov: https://science.nasa.gov/resource/apollo-11-landing-site/
3. The Moon has only a very thin exosphere; no weather. — science.nasa.gov: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/
4. The constant rain of micrometeorites grinds away all airless planetary surfaces. — science.nasa.gov: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/moon/history-of-lunar-exploration/
5. The Moon erodes at a rate of roughly 1 millimeter per million years. — science.nasa.gov: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/moon/history-of-lunar-exploration/
6. LRO photographed Apollo landing sites; astronaut tracks and descent stages are visible. — science.nasa.gov: https://science.nasa.gov/resource/apollo-11-landing-site/

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Animation: code-rendered, no stock footage. Sources are listed per claim; each page should be opened by a person before posting.

One More Orbit: One minute, one 'whoa' about the universe, every number sourced.
